articles.fullText:
The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations (UN) Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital of Yerevan has entered its final stretch.
The conference has adopted 14 decisions and secured more than $1.8 billion in financial commitments. Yet negotiators remain divided over some of the most contentious issues, including who should bear the cost of protecting nature and how global commitments can be translated into measurable results.
With the conference due to conclude on Friday, the focus has shifted from reaffirming global biodiversity goals to reaching agreement on how to achieve them.
Participants attend the COP 17 to the CBD in Yerevan, Armenia, October 27, 2026. 
Tangible progress
The COP17 marks the first global review of progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022 with 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
There are encouraging signs of international cooperation, said Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity, noting that nearly 90% of the convention's parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than 70% have submitted national reports.
The negotiations have also yielded concrete results. Parties have adopted 14 decisions under the convention, covering areas such as invasive alien species, biosafety, gender equality and education.
Funding announcements have added to the summit's momentum, with new commitments from governments, philanthropic organizations and other partners.
The Executive Council of the China-initiated Kunming Biodiversity Fund has approved nine biodiversity conservation projects worth roughly $4.5 million for developing nations, Dong Baotong, vice minister of China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment, said Monday.
China has contributed 400 million yuan (about $60 million) to the fund, which supports biodiversity conservation in developing countries. Schomaker depicted the initiative as an agile instrument for channeling support to where it is needed.
Elsewhere, nine philanthropic organizations pledged $500 million through 2030 for species recovery, while the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund secured over $60 million in new pledges.
These achievements demonstrate that environmental multilateralism is continuing to deliver, even amid profound geopolitical shifts, said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
"Nature is not a luxury we protect when economies can afford it," said Andersen. "Nature is what makes economies possible."
An installation sits outside the venue during the COP 17 to the CBD in Yerevan, Armenia, October 27, 2026. 
Obstacles ahead
Securing new financial commitments is one thing; establishing a sustainable, long-term funding model for biodiversity conservation is another.
Despite the pledges announced in Yerevan, countries remain divided over who should contribute to international biodiversity finance, how much they should pay and how the funds should be allocated.
Other sticking points include reforming subsidies and incentives that harm nature, arrangements for indigenous peoples and local communities, and aligning biodiversity action with climate commitments and other international obligations.
Andersen said ministers are attending the conference's final week to help break the deadlock, particularly on resource mobilization and the global review.
"Financing the destruction of nature with 30 dollars against every dollar spent restoring it is like paying 30 people to tear down your house for every one hired to rebuild it," Schomaker said, framing the way forward around three priorities: accountability, alignment and acceleration.
According to Schomaker, "accountability" means identifying where countries are falling short through national reporting and scientific evidence, while "acceleration" means stepping up efforts to meet the framework's 2030 targets. "Alignment" may prove the hardest part, requiring governments to ensure that public budgets, private investment, economic policies and financial incentives reinforce rather than undermine biodiversity objectives.
The private sector is already pressing for change. More than 130 businesses and financial institutions have called for faster reform of incentives harmful to biodiversity.
Yet, for companies and investors, uncertainty remains over how global biodiversity targets will translate into national regulations, investment requirements and standards for measuring conservation results. Without clearer and more consistent rules, even a growing willingness to invest in nature may struggle to produce results at scale.
Meanwhile, the environmental pressures driving the negotiations are intensifying. UNEP's latest Emissions Gap Report warns that global warming could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius this century under current policies, with potentially severe consequences for ecosystems and biodiversity.
The United Nations' State of Biodiversity Action report, released ahead of COP17, found that fewer than half of the national biodiversity targets assessed by countries were on track.
Against this backdrop, much now hinges on the proposed "Yerevan Pathway," a document that identifies measurable priorities to address gaps in implementing global biodiversity targets over the next two years.
The conference has already shown that multilateral cooperation can deliver decisions and mobilize resources. Whether it can also resolve the harder questions of financing and implementation will be the real test of its success.
"COP17 will be judged by the long-term results we achieve together after the conference, rather than the number of statements made in Yerevan," said Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.

The Hukou Waterfall on the Yellow River, once depicted on China's fourth-series 50-yuan banknotes as a torrent of muddy, turbulent water, now presents a markedly different scene, with its cascading waters running clear.
"Over the past decade, clear cascades at the waterfall have been my main photographic subject," Lyu said. "The contrast with the old scenes is striking."
The Hukou Waterfall, China. 
The reverse side of China's fourth-series 50-yuan banknote, exhibited at the China Numismatic Museum, Beijing, China, September 25, 2024. 
The changing waterscape reflects decades of efforts to protect and manage the Yellow River, China's second-longest river, which flows 5,464 km from its source in the highlands of northwest China's Qinghai Province through nine provinces and autonomous regions, crossing deserts and loess lands before emptying into the Bohai Sea in Shandong Province, east China.
In 1946, under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, an agency for people's Yellow River management was established on the river's banks in Heze, Shandong.e was frequently affected by flooding on the river, the Yellow River Conservancy Commission (YRCC) later moved its headquarters to Zhengzhou in December 1953.
Thanks to 80 years of conservation efforts, the river, once prone to devastating floods, heavy sedimentation and shifting channels, now has cleaner waters and more sustainable water use.
An ecological dyke on the Yellow River in Yuncheng, Shanxi Province, north China, June 10, 2026. 
Historical records show that before the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the river's lower reaches experienced more than 1,500 dyke breaches and overflows and changed course 26 times. Sediment was a persistent challenge, giving rise to the old saying that half of a bowl of Yellow River water is sand.
Wei Xiangyang, the commission's chief engineer, outlined progress in flood control, a central part of river management.
Dykes built to withstand major floods now stretch 1,371 km in total along the lower reaches. Forty flood-control reservoirs on the river and its tributaries have a combined flood-control capacity of 19 billion cubic meters.
Over the past eight decades, these infrastructure projects have helped avoid an estimated 10.09 trillion yuan (around $1.5 trillion) in economic losses from floods, Wei said.
Efforts to curb soil erosion have also produced substantial results. Zhu Xiaoyong, director of the commission's soil and water conservation bureau, presented data showing that 290,500 square km of land affected by soil erosion across the river basin have been rehabilitated. Soil and water conservation measures have kept about 24.7 billion tonnes of sediment from entering the river.
The Yellow River in Luoyang, Henan Province, central China, May 30, 2026. 
The Yellow River spans multiple regions and forms an integrated ecosystem that requires coordinated cross-regional management.
"After years of research, we have developed a reservoir operation approach that stores clean water while discharging sediment," said Zhang Jinliang, chief scientist of Yellow River Engineering Consulting Co., Ltd. "Precision water-sediment regulation marks a shift from passive response to proactive action in managing the river."
Water allocation has also achieved better coordination. Since a unified water-management system covering all provincial-level regions along the river was introduced in 1999, the Yellow River has flowed uninterrupted for 27 consecutive years.
Over the years, more efficient water use has helped expand irrigated farmland in the river basin to 8.8 million hectares. The basin and downstream irrigation areas produce roughly 89.5 billion kilograms of grain annually, or 13.3% of China's national grain output.
YRCC figures also show that water quality in the Yellow River Basin has markedly improved. The proportion of monitoring sections graded Class I to III, indicating good water quality, rose from 59.1% in 2016 to 93.2% in 2025.
Flocks of water birds at the Yellow River Delta in Shandong Province, east China. 
The benefits of conservation are also evident in the lower reaches of the river. At the Yellow River Delta National Nature Reserve in Shandong, 407 bird species have been recorded. Over the past five years, 241 km of waterways have been connected, while ecological water replenishment totaling 860 million cubic meters has helped improve the integrity and biodiversity of the estuary ecosystem.
The changes are also visible in communities along the river. Lyu's photographs documenting the Hukou Waterfall's shifting waterscape have helped boost local tourism. His widely shared photos have helped turn tourism into a pillar industry in a county that was once impoverished.
"The Yellow River ecosystem forms an integrated whole," he said. "From headwater conservation in the upper reaches and soil and water conservation in the middle reaches to wetland restoration in the lower reaches, green has become a defining feature of high-quality development in the Yellow River Basin."

Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks with Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema in Beijing on Friday.
The two leaders announced the elevation of bilateral relations to a China-Gabon community with a shared future for the new era.
Noting that China is willing to be a reliable friend and partner for Gabon in its independent development, Xi said China supports Gabon in maintaining independence in political, economic and diplomatic affairs and will join hands with Gabon to build a China-Gabon community with a shared future for the new era.
Xi said China is ready to work with Gabon to maintain close communication at all levels, exchange experience in political party and state governance and support Gabon in strengthening its governance capacity.
Hailing the strong economic complementarity and great potential for cooperation between the two countries, Xi called on both sides to strengthen the alignment of their development strategies and cultivate new growth drivers for cooperation.
He called for making good use of the new opportunities presented by zero-tariff treatment of African goods and the "green channel" facilitation measures for African agricultural and food products exported to China.
Both sides should expand and upgrade bilateral trade and investment cooperation to support Gabon's industrial development, job creation and livelihood improvement, thereby enhancing the country's capacity for independent economic development, Xi said.
"The vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity and the four major global initiatives I have proposed serve, first and foremost, the common interests of the Global South and African countries," Xi said, adding that China supports Gabon in playing a greater role in international and regional affairs.
Nguema said Gabon firmly adheres to the one-China principle and hopes to draw on China's successful experience in governance of party and country.
He said Gabon stands ready to further deepen practical cooperation with China and welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest and do business in Gabon to help the country achieve industrialization and sustainable development.
Noting that China has established a mutually beneficial and win-win partnership with Africa, Nguema said the zero-tariff policy meets the needs of African countries, enabling African products to enter the vast Chinese market, which is of historic significance to the development of African countries.
He added that Gabon is willing to work with China to enhance solidarity and cooperation between Africa and China and jointly safeguard the interests of Global South countries.
After the talks, the two heads of state witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents covering the implementation of the Global Security Initiative, zero-tariff treatment, industrial and supply chains, Chinese language education and other fields.
During Nguema's state visit to China, the two sides issued a joint statement on building a China-Gabon community with a shared future for the new era.
Prior to the talks, Xi held a welcome ceremony for Nguema in the Great Hall of the People. Xi also held a welcome banquet for him in the evening.
